identification.summary: Microsoft describes Storm-0485 as a prolific phishing operator [S1]. Microsoft tracked it directing targets to Evilginx, an open-source adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) phishing framework [S1]. Microsoft's naming feed lists it as a group in development [S2].
identification.notes: Microsoft's only public description found is the 2025-05-29 blog, which says Evilginx was used by multiple actors 'in the past year', including Storm-0485 and the Russian espionage actor Star Blizzard [S1]. That is a statement about Evilginx use in general and does not date Storm-0485's first activity. No evidence of state sponsorship was found; the actor is described only as a phishing operator [S1]. No aliases are listed by Microsoft [S2].

targeting.notes: Microsoft's description names no sectors, regions or victim organizations for this actor, only generic 'targets' [S1].

capabilities.summary: Microsoft tracked Storm-0485 directing targets to Evilginx AiTM infrastructure [S1]. Observed lure themes were payment remittance, shared documents and fake LinkedIn account verification ('Account Action Required' with a 'Verify Account' button), all designed to prompt a quick response [S1]. Microsoft says the actor consistently passes initial links through obfuscated Google Accelerated Mobile Pages (AMP) URLs to make them harder to identify as malicious [S1].

campaigns.name: Evilginx AiTM phishing reported by Microsoft
campaigns.summary: Microsoft publicly describes Storm-0485 phishing that used Evilginx infrastructure with remittance, shared-document and fake LinkedIn verification lures and obfuscated Google AMP links. The post gives no campaign dates, victims or volumes [S1].

diamond.adversary: Prolific phishing operator, sponsor and motivation not stated by Microsoft [S1].
diamond.capability: Evilginx AiTM phishing; payment, document-sharing and fake LinkedIn lures; link obfuscation through Google AMP URLs [S1].
diamond.infrastructure: Evilginx proxy infrastructure and obfuscated Google AMP URLs used as first-hop links [S1].
diamond.technology: Credential and session theft against accounts protected by MFA is the general AiTM risk Microsoft describes in the same post; the post's mitigation guidance is the source for defenders [S1].

gaps: Only one substantive primary source (Microsoft, 2025-05-29) was found. Searches for 'Storm-0485' returned no vendor or government reporting beyond it.
Victim sectors, regions, volumes, motivation (criminal vs. espionage) and sponsor are not stated in the sources gathered.

First-observed date and any predecessor DEV-0485 designation could not be verified; one search summary suggested DEV-#### names were succeeded by Storm-#### names generally, but no source tying DEV-0485 to this actor was found.
Microsoft's April 2025 monthly news item and the Microsoft threat-actor naming page appeared in search results but could not be opened (fetch failed), so they are not cited.
Overlaps with other Evilginx users (for example Star Blizzard) are not evidence of a shared cluster; Microsoft names them as separate actors [S1].
